# SPS Commerce (SPSC) — A Deep Dive on Management and the Setup

*Forensic dossier · five consecutive quarterly calls (Q1 2025 through Q1 2026) cross-referenced against the screener financials · live price $63.40 (NASDAQ, 2026-07-13), down about 56% from the 52-week high of $143.55.*

SPS Commerce runs the largest retail supply-chain network in North America — a cloud service that lets retailers and their suppliers exchange orders, shipments and invoices electronically (the industry calls this EDI, electronic data interchange). It has now grown revenue for 100 consecutive quarters. The stock, however, has been cut in half over the past year. This dossier tests whether that fall is a fear-print on a durable franchise or the market correctly pricing a broken growth story.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management told across these five calls changed materially, and the change is the whole thesis.

**Early 2025 (Q1–Q2): unbroken compounder.** The opening quarters were vintage SPS. First-quarter 2025 revenue grew 21% to $181.5M, the "97th consecutive quarter of revenue growth"; second quarter grew 22%. Management leaned into its network story — over 50,000 trading partners, an "$11 billion total addressable market" — and framed its February 2025 acquisition of Carbon6 as establishing "a clear leader in the emerging category of revenue recovery." Revenue recovery (software that recovers money retailers wrongly deduct from suppliers) was positioned as the next growth leg.

**Mid-2025 (Q2–Q3): the first cracks.** By the second-quarter call, management introduced a new phrase that would recur every quarter thereafter — "heightened spend scrutiny and delayed purchasing decisions" among suppliers, attributed to tariff and macro uncertainty. It was explicitly a U.S. supplier phenomenon ("we have not seen the same level of spend scrutiny in Europe and Australia"). The third-quarter call then delivered the first real miss inside the story: the revenue-recovery business came in "approximately $3 million below our expectations," undone by "seasonality" and "a change in Amazon policy related to inventory capacity for third-party sellers." The acquired growth engine had a hair in it.

**Late 2025–early 2026 (Q4–Q1 2026): the narrative inverts.** Full-year 2025 revenue grew 18% to $751.5M, but the guide for 2026 was a shock to the model — roughly 7% growth ($798.5M–$806.9M), and just 6% in the first quarter. The company that had never printed below double digits in living memory was guiding to mid-single digits. Management reframed the story around two ideas: (1) the weakness is "transitory," concentrated in Amazon 3P revenue recovery and in tariff-driven spend scrutiny that will be "largely behind us by the end of the second quarter"; and (2) the future is a pivot from winning new customers to expanding revenue per existing customer (ARPU), aided by a new AI agent, "MAX," and a reorganized go-to-market team under a new Chief Commercial Officer. The most important structural move came just after the last call in this set: on 2026-06-30 SPS **completed the sale of the 3P Revenue Recovery business** — surgically removing the very asset (acquired barely 16 months earlier via Carbon6) that had become the growth drag.

The arc, then, is a clean compounder that made one bad acquisition into a melting end-market (Amazon third-party sellers), watched macro spend-scrutiny stack on top of it, guided the market down hard, and has now cut out the bad limb while promising a second-half-2026 reacceleration.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The financial evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "100th consecutive quarter of revenue growth" (Q4 2025) | Revenue: $385M (2021) → $451M → $537M → $638M → $752M (2025), a clean 18.6% three-year compound rate. | **Holds.** The durability is real and rare. |
| Growth is decelerating only "transitorily" | Growth ran 21–22% in H1 2025, fell to 16% in Q3, 13% in Q4, and is guided to ~6–7% for all of 2026. Latest-quarter EPS was **down 9% year over year**. | **Partly holds, partly unproven.** The deceleration is undeniable and steep; "transitory" is a forward promise, not yet a fact. |
| Margins keep expanding | Gross margin 64.2% and rising; adjusted EBITDA grew 24% in 2025 to $231.4M (~31% margin) even as revenue grew 18%; 2026 EBITDA guided up 13–15% to ~$263M (~33% margin) on just 7% revenue growth. | **Holds strongly.** This is the tell of a real franchise — profit is growing roughly twice as fast as revenue. |
| Disciplined capital allocation | Net cash position of about $148M (cash $154M vs $7M total debt); **76% of 2025 free cash flow returned via $115M of buybacks**; repurchase authorization raised to $300M; $47M bought in Q1 2026 alone. | **Holds.** Aggressive, price-sensitive buyback into the drawdown. |

The returns understate the economics. |

Where the story is **richer than the numbers**: the "AI moat" and MAX-agent narrative is early and unmonetized (a 400-customer beta). Where the story is **poorer than the numbers**: the market is pricing SPSC as if the 7% growth is terminal, yet the margin trajectory and cash generation say the franchise is intact.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Declining, then stabilizing.** The shift from offensive to defensive language is measurable quarter by quarter. Q1 2025 was pure offense — "strong start," TAM expansion, "uniquely positioned." By Q2–Q3 the vocabulary turned defensive and hedged: "closely monitoring," "spend scrutiny," "delayed purchasing decisions." Guidance specificity actually improved (management began breaking out 1P vs 3P customer counts and quantifying the revenue-recovery shortfall to the dollar), which reads as candor rather than evasion. By Q1 2026 the tone had steadied into a "we see the bottom" posture — "early indications that the invoice scrutiny... is subsiding," headwinds "largely behind us by the end of the second quarter." Confidence is no longer swaggering, but it is specific and internally consistent.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High, with one important caveat.** The screener records a 7-for-7 earnings-beat rate, and the call history corroborates a house style of setting beatable bars — Q1 2025 EBITDA beat, Q1 2026 non-GAAP EPS of $1.10 topped the $0.97 consensus. Management held the full-year 2025 revenue guide steady through the tariff scare (Q1 and Q2 both reaffirmed the range) and then delivered $751.5M inside it. The caveat is the revenue-recovery line specifically: they guided it up when they bought Carbon6, missed it by $3M in Q3 2025, discovered "more seasonality... than we had originally anticipated," and have now sold the worst part of it. On their *core* business the guidance track record is strong; on the *acquired* business it was poor — which is precisely why divesting it improves the signal quality of everything they guide from here.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts circled three themes relentlessly. **First, the durability of customer adds** — Jeff Van Rhee and Nehal Chokshi pushed for quarters on whether organic customer count could "go negative," and management repeatedly deflected to the timing of "community enablement" (now "relationship management") campaigns, which later did soften (1P adds went flat in Q4). **Second, the revenue-recovery/Amazon exposure** — Joe Vruwink pressed on whether the $3M Q3 shortfall annualized to a double-digit haircut on that business; management conceded it would grow slower but stayed vague. That pressure point became the news: the business was ultimately sold. **Third, the 2026 growth inflection** — on the Q1 2026 call Chokshi pointedly asked why the back half should reaccelerate if the core ex-Amazon business is "already at high single digits," and management's answer rested entirely on *lapping* the 2025 headwinds rather than on new demand. That is the single unresolved question the numbers cannot yet settle.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 Growth collapsed from ~21% (Q1 2025) to a ~7% guide (2026) — a genuine step-down, not noise.
🔴 The Carbon6 acquisition was a capital-allocation misstep: bought Feb 2025, its 3P core sold ~16 months later after seasonality and Amazon policy blew up the thesis.
🔴 Insider behaviour is one-sided: zero open-market buys against 42 sells (~49,500 shares) — no management conviction signal at these prices.
🔴 The long-tenured Chief Financial Officer, Kim Nelson, is departing (announced Q3 2025) — a loss of continuity at the top of finance.
🟢 100 consecutive quarters of revenue growth; the network has never shrunk.
🟢 Margins expanding through the downturn — EBITDA up 24% in 2025, guided up 13–15% in 2026.
🟢 Net cash and 76% of free cash flow returned as buybacks into the fall — accretive at a depressed multiple.
🟢 The problem business has been surgically removed (3P Revenue Recovery sold 2026-06-30), cleaning the growth signal.
🟢 An activist investor is pushing, and the company is exploring a sale (Reuters, 2026-06-23) — an external forcing function.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling terminology shift is the quiet rebrand of "community enablement" into "relationship management," coincident with management admitting that new-customer adds would no longer be the primary growth driver — ARPU expansion would. Read plainly: the network is maturing, and management is repositioning the story from *acquisition* to *monetization* before the market forces the point. A second signal is the new-executive influx — a Chief Commercial Officer (Eduardo Rosini, ex-Sage/Intuit/Microsoft) from December 2025 and a new Chief Marketing Officer — imported specifically to build "operational rigor" and a cross-sell muscle the founder-era organization lacked. This is a company being professionalized for a different phase (and, plausibly, for a sale). The AI framing (MAX) is dual-purpose: pitched to customers as new value, but management is equally explicit that AI is cutting its own onboarding cost "from weeks to days" and that "much of our software development" is now agent-driven — i.e., AI is a margin lever as much as a revenue one.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE, tilting toward PIVOTING.** This is not a deteriorating franchise — it is a high-quality network compounder that absorbed one bad acquisition and a macro spend-scrutiny air-pocket, guided the market down honestly, and has now excised the damaged asset while an activist forces a strategic review. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **the entire re-rating case rests on an unproven second-half-2026 growth reacceleration that management attributes to *lapping* 2025 headwinds, not to observed new demand.** If Q2 2026 confirms the inflection, the current ~8x EV/EBITDA (enterprise value to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) on a net-cash 33%-margin compounder is far too cheap. If the "transitory" weakness proves structural, the low multiple is deserved.

**Moat:** a genuine network-and-switching-cost moat. EDI compliance is mission-critical, contractually sticky, and priced too low (management notes it is "not priced on GMV") to be worth cutting — churn stayed "very consistent" even through the tariff scare. The 64% and rising gross margin and the profit-growing-faster-than-revenue pattern are the signatures of a moat that is intact, not eroding. The AI question (could large language models disintermediate EDI?) is real but distant: SPS's asset is a hard-wired network of tens of thousands of trading relationships and decades of transaction data, closer to a toll road than to thin-switching-cost horizontal software. I judge the moat wide and stable, and any secular threat manageable rather than terminal — the cheapness here is a fear-print, not a melting base.

bull_thesis:
SPS Commerce owns the plumbing of American retail. Roughly 55,000 suppliers, retailers and logistics firms exchange their orders, shipping notices and invoices across its network using electronic data interchange, or EDI — the standardised digital format that lets a supplier and a retailer talk to each other without a human retyping anything. The company has now grown revenue for 100 consecutive quarters, a 25-year streak spanning two recessions, a pandemic and a tariff shock. The bull case is that the market has confused a growth reset with a business problem, and is selling a durable network at a price that invites someone to buy the whole thing.

Start with what actually broke. Revenue growth fell from 18% in 2025 to a guided 7% for 2026, and the shares fell about 54% from their 52-week high of $143.55 to $65.75 today. But the core Fulfillment product — the EDI network itself — grew 8% in the first quarter of 2026 while the consolidated line grew 6%. The damage came from two identifiable, dated events, neither of which is the network failing. First, a tariff-driven cost-cutting cycle among suppliers: management described customers 'really studying the invoice they get from SPS Commerce' looking for savings (third quarter 2025), and said in the first quarter of 2026 there are 'early indications that the invoice scrutiny we observed last year... is subsiding,' expecting the drag 'largely behind us by the end of the second quarter.' Second, Amazon unilaterally changed marketplace policies in a way that gutted the revenue-recovery business acquired through Carbon6 — and on 30 June 2026 the company sold that third-party piece outright for $9.5 million cash, taking an estimated $20 million loss. The problem asset is gone. What remains is the network.

The network's economics are genuinely good and getting better. Gross margin is 64.2% and rising, on a mechanism management explained specifically and has delivered against: automating customer onboarding so the business needs fewer people per customer (third and fourth quarters of 2025). Adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA — a rough proxy for operating cash generation) grew 24% in 2025 on 18% revenue growth, and is guided to grow 13-15% in 2026 on 7% revenue growth. That two-points-a-year margin expansion is the one forward commitment management has kept every single time. Churn is 'very consistent' even through the tariff shock (second quarter 2025) and per-connection pricing is 'consistent' with no discounting (fourth quarter 2025) — a business losing its moat does not hold price through a customer cost-cutting drive. The balance sheet carries net cash of $148 million against essentially no debt, and the Altman-Z solvency score of 8.7 says there is no financing risk in this equity at all.

The switching costs are structural, not habitual. As Chad Collins put it in the first quarter of 2025, a supplier's EDI connection is 'the way that these [suppliers are] getting their orders from their customers, so it's a pretty important piece of their business.' You do not rip that out to save a few thousand dollars a year. And the network compounds on both sides: retailers run enablement drives because SPS already holds their suppliers, and suppliers join because SPS already holds their retailers.

The valuation is the crux. On enterprise value to EBITDA with stock-based compensation properly expensed — the apples-to-apples basis a buyer actually underwrites — SPS trades at 12.5 times. Descartes Systems trades at 19.0 times, Kinaxis at 19.9 times, Manhattan Associates at 31.9 times (all live, 16 July 2026). Free cash flow over the trailing twelve months was $167 million against a $2.41 billion market value.

Then the catalyst. Reuters reported on 23 June 2026 that SPS has retained Morgan Stanley to explore a sale under pressure from two activist investors — Anson Funds, which signed a cooperation agreement in February 2026, and Irenic Capital, whose stake surfaced in January 2026 — with private-equity firms the expected buyers. Read backwards, the last three quarters are the standard pre-sale grooming sequence: stop acquiring, start buying back stock at scale ($115 million in 2025, 76% of free cash flow; $47 million in the first quarter of 2026; authorisation lifted to $300 million), refresh the executive bench, sell the broken asset. This is a near-perfect private-equity target: a net-cash balance sheet, 33% margins, 95%-plus retention, recurring revenue, and roughly $67 million of annual stock compensation a private owner would convert to a fraction of that in cash pay — instantly lifting the earnings a buyer underwrites. The environment is as friendly as it has been in years: record first-half 2026 merger activity of about $2.8 trillion, $3.7 trillion of private-equity money waiting to be deployed, and high-yield borrowing spreads at 278 basis points near cycle tights.

Conditions the bull case requires: that the second-half 2026 reacceleration management has guided to actually appears in the 30 July print; that the sale process produces a bidder rather than a press release; that AI compresses the cost of running the network faster than it compresses what SPS can charge for it; and that the new chief financial officer, who has already declined to raise the guide he inherited, is setting a floor rather than managing expectations down.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that SPS Commerce is a bad business. It is that you would be buying a fair-priced 7% grower at a price that has already been bid up 21% on an unconfirmed rumour, in a business whose central selling point is precisely the thing artificial intelligence is best at destroying.

Start with the price you are paying. The stock was $54.44 on 23 June 2026 when Reuters reported the sale exploration. It is $65.75 today, 17% above its 50-day average and 34% off its 52-week low of $49.04. Nothing has been confirmed by the company. There are no terms, no price, no deadline, and no obligation on anyone to transact. The activists who generated this idea have already been paid for it. What is left for a new buyer is the residual — and if the process ends without a deal, which is the single most common outcome of 'exploring a sale,' the shares do not fall to some structural floor. They fall back toward the $49-54 the market set before the leak. There is no net cash cushion worth naming here: $148 million across 36.7 million shares is about $4 a share.

Now the structural risk, which is the reason the whole complex de-rated and is not a story about tariffs. SPS's own stated differentiator, from the second quarter of 2025, is being 'the only full-service EDI solution on the market.' Read that honestly: the product is substantially managed human labour — mapping documents, onboarding suppliers, keeping compliance current as retailers change their requirements. That is the work. And management has now confirmed, on its own call, that AI collapses exactly that work: in the first quarter of 2026 Collins said AI has cut SPS's 'onboarding and setup time from weeks to days' and that 'much of our software development [is] now agent-driven.' What is good for the margin line is dangerous for the price line. If AI agents make EDI integration cheap for SPS, they make it cheap for competitors and for customers' own internal teams. The full-service premium — the thing the ARPU rests on — has a ceiling on it that did not exist three years ago. The tell is in the transcripts: every AI passage describes SPS getting cheaper to run; not one describes SPS getting harder to leave. When Jackson Bogli asked directly in the third quarter of 2025 about AI 'building that competitive moat,' the answer was entirely about internal cost efficiency and said nothing about defending pricing. When Jeff Van Rhee circled the EDI-versus-API question in the fourth quarter of 2025, he got a deflection.

Management's forward claims have a poor record, and specifically on everything they bought. In the second quarter of 2025, unprompted, Kim Nelson volunteered a medium-term floor of 'at least high single digits' growth beyond 2025. Two quarters later the 2026 guide was 7%; the first quarter of 2026 delivered 6%. Full-year 2025 was guided to $758.5-763 million in the first quarter of 2025, reaffirmed at $759-763 million in the second quarter, and landed at $751.5 million — a miss against a range they twice declined to lower while narrating the very headwinds that caused it. Carbon6 was announced as having 'established SPS as a clear leader in the emerging category of revenue recovery' (first quarter 2025); it was closed without a complete customer list, an admission management presented as good news; it produced 'net zero' customer adds within six weeks of closing; its seasonality was mis-modelled eight months in ('we now recognize that there is more seasonality in this business than we had originally anticipated,' third quarter 2025); management expressed 'strong conviction' it would outgrow the core in 2026 (third quarter 2025); and the third-party portion was sold sixteen months after purchase for $9.5 million at a $20 million loss. That is a complete capital-destruction cycle, and it is the single best available evidence of what this team does with cash.

The seven-of-seven earnings beat rate is not skill, it is policy — and it beats on non-GAAP earnings per share, the line management controls through cost discipline. # SPS Commerce (SPSC) — Forensic Dossier

*Interrogator pass, 2026-07-17. Sources: five consecutive earnings calls (Q1 2025 through Q1 2026), the screener's financial trajectory, live market data from FMP, and dated public filings/news. Share price used throughout: $65.75 (NASDAQ, US dollars, 2026-07-16 close).*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

SPS Commerce runs the largest retail supply-chain network in the world — roughly 55,000 suppliers, retailers and logistics firms exchanging orders, shipping notices and invoices through an electronic data interchange, or EDI (the standardised digital plumbing that lets a supplier and a retailer talk to each other automatically). Over these five calls the story mutated three times, and each mutation was a retreat from the prior one.

**Act one (Q1–Q2 2025) — the expansion story.** The company was compounding at 21–22% and buying its way into a new category. Chad Collins opened Q1 2025 with the Carbon6 acquisition having "established SPS as a clear leader in the emerging category of revenue recovery" — revenue recovery being the business of clawing back money retailers deduct from supplier invoices for late or incorrect shipments. Management sized an "$11 billion total addressable market" and leaned on the growth flywheel: run enablement campaigns (organised drives that push a retailer's supplier base onto the network), collect new subscribers, then upsell them more connections. The tone was expansionary and the numbers backed it: Q1 2025 revenue $181.5M (+21%), Q2 2025 $187.4M (+22%).

**Act two (Q2 2025 → Q4 2025) — the quiet reset.** The pivotal moment is buried in the Q2 2025 prepared remarks, where Kim Nelson volunteered a medium-term commitment: "at least high single digits" growth beyond 2025. Read in sequence, that was not guidance — it was a controlled demolition of the 20% growth narrative, delivered while the company was still printing 22%. From there the story became defensive: "heightened spend scrutiny and delayed purchasing decisions" (Q2 2025), then a $3M revenue-recovery miss and a seasonality confession in Q3 2025, then a Q4 2025 guide of just 7% growth for 2026 — below the "at least high single digits" floor management had set only two quarters earlier. Growth drivers were quietly re-ranked: at the Q2 2025 call the "largest opportunity" was still upselling connections; by Q3 2025 the mix explicitly shifted to "a larger portion of that growth would be coming from the ARPU side" (ARPU = average revenue per user, the annual spend per customer). Customer adds — the metric the entire flywheel narrative rested on — went from the hero to the sidekick.

**Act three (Q1 2026) — the AI re-skin and the capital-allocation pivot.** The company rebranded itself as "the leading intelligent supply chain network" and introduced MAX, an AI agent, with 400-plus beta customers. Simultaneously, the M&A narrative that defined act one was abandoned in a single sentence: "The most efficient use of our capital today is buying back shares." The 3P revenue-recovery business — the Amazon-marketplace assets acquired via Carbon6 sixteen months earlier — was first repriced with a "subscription platform fee" (Q1 2026), then sold outright on 2026-06-30 for $9.5M cash at an estimated $20M loss.

**What was dropped without ceremony:** the $11B TAM figure; the "clear leader in revenue recovery" framing; the customer-count flywheel as the primary growth engine; and the "at least high single digits" medium-term floor.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING.** Not deteriorating — the core network grew 8% last quarter, margins are expanding on schedule, the balance sheet holds net cash, and 100 consecutive quarters of revenue growth is not the signature of a business in decline. But this is no longer the company that reported Q1 2025. Inside sixteen months it has replaced most of its executive team, stopped acquiring, started buying back stock at scale, sold the asset it called a category win, renamed its central growth programme, re-described itself as an AI company, and — per Reuters on 2026-06-23 — hired a banker to explore selling itself. Every one of those is a pivot, and they all point the same direction.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing:** *you would be buying the leak, not the news.* The stock was $54.44 when Reuters broke the sale story on 2026-06-23; it is $65.75 today — a 21% move on a report the company has never confirmed, with no terms, no price, no deadline, and no obligation on anyone to transact. The activists have already been paid for their idea. What remains is the residual: a good business at a fair-to-modestly-cheap price, plus a lottery ticket whose cost has risen 21% since it was issued. If the process ends without a deal — which is the single most common outcome of "exploring a sale" — the floor is not the current price, it is somewhere nearer the $49–54 the market set before the leak. Size it as a quality holding that might get taken out, never as an arbitrage, because there is nothing here to arbitrage.

**Economic moat: NARROW, trend STABLE.** The moat type is switching-costs layered on a network. Both legs are real. The switching costs are structural: a supplier's EDI connection is, in Collins's own Q1 2025 words, "the way that these [suppliers are] getting their orders from their customers, so it's a pretty important piece of their business" — you do not rip that out to save a few thousand dollars a year. The network leg compounds: retailers run enablement campaigns *because* SPS already has their suppliers, and suppliers join *because* SPS already has their retailers. The evidence supports width on the core and denies it on the whole: churn is "very consistent" (Q2 2025) even through a tariff shock; per-connection pricing is "consistent" (Q4 2025) with no discounting; gross margin is 64% and rising, not falling; adjusted EBITDA margin is expanding two points a year on plan. That combination — stable pricing, rising margins, stable churn, 100 straight quarters — is not an eroding moat. It is a narrow one holding its ground. What keeps it narrow rather than wide: consolidated return on invested capital is only 8.7%, growth has decelerated to 6%, and the moat demonstrably does not extend beyond the core — SPS bought two adjacent businesses and the network conferred no protection on either.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** The force is generative-AI displacement, and the specific mechanism matters more than the headline. SPS's stated differentiator is being "the only full-service EDI solution on the market" (Q2 2025) — the product is substantially *managed human labour*: mapping documents, onboarding suppliers, keeping compliance current as retailers change requirements. Management has now confirmed on its own call that AI compresses exactly that labour, cutting SPS's "onboarding and setup time from weeks to days" (Q1 2026). What is good for SPS's margin is dangerous for SPS's price: if AI agents make EDI integration cheap for SPS, they make it cheap for rivals and for customers' internal teams, which caps the full-service premium and eventually the ARPU. That is a real ceiling on pricing power and it is the reason the entire supply-chain software complex has de-rated — Descartes is 30% off its high, Manhattan Associates 34% off, and SPS 54% off. But it is not terminal, and the distinction is load-bearing. AI does not replace the *network*. Two counterparties still need to agree on a standard, and the value of being the hub where 55,000 of them already agreed is not something a language model manufactures. Every AI passage in these transcripts is about SPS getting cheaper to run; none is about SPS getting harder to leave — that silence is the honest measure of the risk. Meanwhile SPS is arguably the AI *beneficiary* on the cost line, and the network data feeding MAX is a genuine asset a competitor cannot synthesise.

**Fear-print or value trap?** Fear-print, with a caveat the director must hold. The base is not structurally shrinking — it grew in its 100th consecutive quarter, and the core Fulfillment product grew 8% while the headline grew 6%. The damage is fully attributable to two identifiable, dated, non-recurring events: a tariff-driven spend-scrutiny cycle management expects to lap by the end of Q2 2026, and Amazon's unilateral policy change to an acquired business that has now been sold. Neither is the network failing. The caveat is that this is a fear-print on a business whose growth algorithm genuinely reset from 18% to 7% and is not going back — so the correct response is a lower multiple, not the old one. The market has delivered a *much* lower multiple: 12.5x enterprise value to EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, with stock compensation properly expensed) against 19–20x for Descartes and Kinaxis and 32x for Manhattan Associates on the identical basis. A roughly 37% discount is more than a 7% grower deserves to give up when it carries net cash, expanding margins and a switching-cost network. That gap is the opportunity — and it is precisely why a private-equity buyer has a banker's phone number.
